Reference: Helpman (1998); Redding and Rossi-Hansberg (2017); Details and Codes

Model Setting

This review article asks how the uneven distribution of economic activity across space can be studied with models that are rich enough to be taken to the data and still tractable enough to deliver general equilibrium counterfactuals. Earlier theoretical work on new economic geography (Krugman 1991; Fujita, Krugman and Venables 1999) aimed at a fundamental explanation of agglomeration: love of variety, increasing returns and transport costs generate cumulative causation and multiple equilibria even on a featureless plain. Its complexity confined the analysis to stylized settings (two or a few symmetric regions, a circle, a line), so the empirical work it inspired was largely reduced form, without a clear structural interpretation of the coefficients. Quantitative spatial models, which follow the quantitative trade model of Eaton and Kortum (2002), have a different aim. Agglomeration is the outcome of exogenous local characteristics augmented by endogenous mechanisms. The models admit many asymmetric locations that differ in productivity, amenities, land and bilateral trade and mobility frictions; they deliver gravity equations for trade and commuting; and they are typically exactly identified, so that observed data can be rationalized as an equilibrium and unobserved fundamentals can be recovered by model inversion. The same reduced-form system arises from a whole class of microfoundations, and conditions for existence and uniqueness of equilibrium are available.

The article has three parts. It gives a taxonomy of the building blocks that such models combine. It then works out two canonical examples: a multiregion version of the Helpman (1998) model, in which regions are linked by costly goods trade and free labor mobility, and a quantitative urban model with commuting in the spirit of Lucas and Rossi-Hansberg (2002) and Ahlfeldt et al. (2015). Finally, it reviews the evidence on market access, density and path dependence. This note concentrates on the first example. For that model the review derives a system in populations alone, shows that a unique equilibrium exists when σ(1−α)>1\sigma(1-\alpha)>1σ(1−α)>1, shows how to recover productivities and land supplies from observed wages and populations, states the exact-hat counterfactual system, and shows that the change in a location's domestic trade share and population is a sufficient statistic for the welfare effect of a change in trade costs. In an illustration on a grid of 900 locations in two countries, removing a border tax of 100 percent raises welfare by 0.2 to 0.3 percent, while removing an internal tax of the same size raises it by 1.4 to 2.3 percent.

Menu of Building Blocks

The review organizes the modeling choices into seven groups and three criteria for choosing among them.

  • Preferences: homogeneous goods (Eaton and Kortum 2002), goods differentiated by origin (Armington 1969) or by firm with love of variety (Krugman 1991; Helpman 1998); one or many sectors; exogenous amenities (Rosen 1979; Roback 1982) or endogenous amenities; a fixed local factor in utility such as residential land, which acts as a dispersion force; and common preferences, which equalize real wages under free mobility, versus idiosyncratic preferences drawn from an extreme value distribution, which give each location an upward-sloping labor supply curve.

  • Production technology: constant versus increasing returns; exogenous versus endogenous productivity; input-output linkages (Krugman and Venables 1995; Caliendo et al. 2014); and fixed local factors in production such as commercial land, which act as a congestion force.

  • Costs of trading goods: iceberg variable costs, where dni>1d_{ni}>1dni​>1 units must be shipped from iii for one unit to arrive in nnn, versus fixed costs; symmetric versus asymmetric costs; geographic frictions (mountains) versus economic frictions (borders, road and rail networks), often measured with lowest-cost-route algorithms; and nontraded goods, the limiting case dni→∞d_{ni}\to\inftydni​→∞. Any plausible model should reproduce the gravity equation.

  • Technology for idea flows: knowledge externalities, usually a function of distance-weighted employment in surrounding locations and empirically highly localized; intentional innovation, which makes the problem dynamic; and the transferability of ideas across locations.

  • Costs of moving people: migration costs, which make location choices forward looking when they are sunk; commuting, which separates workplace and residence; common versus idiosyncratic preferences or productivities and multiple worker types, which produce gravity in migration and commuting and spatial sorting; and congestion in transportation.

  • Endowments: homogeneous or heterogeneous labor; the spatial scope and the spatial units (city blocks, counties, regions, countries); immobile land; capital and transport infrastructure, the latter mostly treated as exogenous.

  • Equilibrium: perfect competition (constant returns) or monopolistic competition (internal increasing returns, with free entry and zero profits); general versus partial equilibrium (a city facing a reservation utility, a country facing world prices); the ownership of land, handled through absentee landlords, a global portfolio, local redistribution to residents, or local immobile landlords; and the spatial unit at which trade is balanced.

  • Criteria: analytical and computational tractability; the choice of structural parameters and location fundamentals that are invariant to the policy studied, without which the analysis is subject to the Lucas critique; and the connection between the model and the available data, including whether the model is exactly identified and invertible and which overidentification checks are possible.

General Equilibrium

The equilibrium is characterized by three sets of relationships: the trade share together with income equal to expenditure (a wage equation), the price index, and the population mobility condition. With symmetric trade costs the review follows Allen and Arkolakis (2014) to reduce them to a system of NNN equations in the NNN populations:

When the kernel is symmetric, the solution has the property that the origin term of one system is proportional to the destination term of the other, and this proportionality is the wage relation above. Substituting it into the price index equation eliminates wages and leaves the system in populations.

Existence and Uniqueness

The population system has the form of a nonlinear fixed-point problem in which the unknown appears with exponent one on the left and with exponent γ2/γ1\gamma_2/\gamma_1γ2​/γ1​ inside the sum. Using results on such systems (Fujimoto and Krause 1985), Allen and Arkolakis (2014) show that there exists a unique LnL_nLn​ for each nnn as long as γ2/γ1∈(0,1)\gamma_2/\gamma_1\in(0,1)γ2​/γ1​∈(0,1). Thus, given {Hn,An}\{H_n,A_n\}{Hn​,An​} and symmetric {dni}\{d_{ni}\}{dni​}, there is a unique equilibrium, and it can be found by iteration from any initial distribution of populations. With continuous space the sum is replaced by an integral and the same conclusions follow from a theorem in Zabreyko et al. (1975).

The review states that a sufficient condition for γ2/γ1∈(0,1)\gamma_2/\gamma_1\in(0,1)γ2​/γ1​∈(0,1) is σ(1−α)>1\sigma(1-\alpha)>1σ(1−α)>1. Direct calculation shows that γ2<γ1\gamma_2<\gamma_1γ2​<γ1​ is equivalent to σ(1−α)>1\sigma(1-\alpha)>1σ(1−α)>1. Positivity of γ2\gamma_2γ2​ is a separate requirement, (2σ−1)/(σ−1)>(σ−1)(1−α)/α(2\sigma-1)/(\sigma-1)>(\sigma-1)(1-\alpha)/\alpha(2σ−1)/(σ−1)>(σ−1)(1−α)/α, which holds at the parameter values used in the illustration (γ1=5/3\gamma_1=5/3γ1​=5/3 and γ2=11/12\gamma_2=11/12γ2​=11/12) but is not implied by σ(1−α)>1\sigma(1-\alpha)>1σ(1−α)>1 in general. Uniqueness is not lost when it fails: γ1+γ2>0\gamma_1+\gamma_2>0γ1​+γ2​>0 always holds, so σ(1−α)>1\sigma(1-\alpha)>1σ(1−α)>1 implies ∣γ2/γ1∣<1|\gamma_2/\gamma_1|<1∣γ2​/γ1​∣<1, which is what the fixed-point argument requires. The restriction guarantees that congestion forces dominate agglomeration forces. As population concentrates in a location, the measure of varieties produced there expands, which with trade costs makes the location a more attractive residence. Concentration also bids up land prices. A higher σ\sigmaσ weakens the agglomeration force, and a higher land share 1−α1-\alpha1−α strengthens the dispersion force. This is the same comparison as the sign of the population exponent in the expression for Vˉ\bar{V}Vˉ.

Uniqueness makes counterfactuals determinate, but it has a cost. Multiple equilibria were a central feature of the earlier theory, as in the core-periphery model of Krugman (1991), and the restriction excludes them. When σ(1−α)>1\sigma(1-\alpha)>1σ(1−α)>1 the model cannot generate agglomeration on a perfectly homogeneous space; agglomerations arise only from initial differences across locations. The review adds that whether a model has multiple equilibria may depend on its level of abstraction: idiosyncratic factors that select one allocation can be interpreted as realizations of a stochastic error, and they are likely to matter more at small spatial scales (blocks within cities) than at large ones (regions or countries).

Isomorphisms

The equilibrium system does not depend on the particular microfoundation. Allen and Arkolakis (2014) demonstrate an isomorphism with a perfectly competitive Armington model, in which goods are differentiated by location of origin, extended to incorporate labor mobility and external economies. Allen and Arkolakis (2014) and Redding (2016) show that similar properties hold in a perfectly competitive Ricardian model in the tradition of Eaton and Kortum (2002) with labor mobility and external economies of scale. The frameworks differ in assumptions (monopolistic versus perfect competition), in mechanisms (pecuniary versus technological externalities) and in the structural interpretation of reduced-form coefficients. In particular, the elasticity of trade with respect to trade costs is σ−1\sigma-1σ−1 here and is the dispersion of productivity in the Ricardian model. They also differ in some predictions: when factors are mobile, reductions in trade costs affect the spatial distribution of activity differently under constant and increasing returns. They agree on a series of predictions such as gravity. The review does not develop a version with heterogeneous firms; it notes only that the spatial literature has paid less attention to fixed trade costs than the trade literature on heterogeneous firms, and that the welfare result below is the analog of the result for the class of trade models in Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare (2012).

Model Inversion

Suppose the researcher has values for α\alphaα and σ\sigmaσ, has parameterized symmetric trade costs dnid_{ni}dni​ (for example as a constant elasticity function of distance), and observes populations {Ln}\{L_n\}{Ln​} and wages {wn}\{w_n\}{wn​}. There is then a one-to-one mapping from the parameters and the observed data to the unobserved {An,Hn}\{A_n,H_n\}{An​,Hn​}, up to a normalization. Solving for an equilibrium uses the population system and the wage relation to find {Ln,wn}\{L_n,w_n\}{Ln​,wn​} given {An,Hn}\{A_n,H_n\}{An​,Hn​}; inversion uses the same two relations in the opposite direction. The wage relation is solved for HnH_nHn​ and substituted into the population system, the resulting system is solved for {An}\{A_n\}{An​}, and {Hn}\{H_n\}{Hn​} is then recovered from the wage relation. The review argues that existence and uniqueness follow from the same fixed-point theorems, provided that after the substitution the exponent on AiA_iAi​ inside the sum is smaller than the exponent on AnA_nAn​ outside the sum, and states that this is guaranteed if σ(1−α)>1\sigma(1-\alpha)>1σ(1−α)>1. Carrying out the substitution, productivity enters as An−(σ−1)A_n^{-(\sigma-1)}An−(σ−1)​ on the left and as Aiσ−1A_i^{\sigma-1}Aiσ−1​ inside the sum, so the two exponents do not depend on α\alphaα. The solution is nevertheless unique up to scale, because the system amounts to scaling a symmetric positive matrix to given row sums. With the recovered productivities, the trade share equation predicts the unobserved bilateral trade shares. If trade shares πni\pi_{ni}πni​ are observed instead, then land supplies, productivities and bilateral trade costs can all be recovered, again up to a normalization.

Three implications follow. First, the model is exactly identified: it has as many unobserved location characteristics as observed endogenous variables, so its ability to match the data is not a test of the model. Second, wages and populations alone cannot identify α\alphaα and σ\sigmaσ, because any change in these parameters can be offset by changes in the recovered fundamentals. Third, since HnH_nHn​ is quality-adjusted land, comparing it with geographical land area only yields a measure of average land quality, which is related to residential amenities. The recovered fundamentals account for the variation in the endogenous variables according to the model but do not explain it. Testing the model or estimating its parameters requires additional data or exogenous shocks.

Counterfactuals

Counterfactuals can be computed from the observed endogenous variables in an initial equilibrium without solving for the unobserved location characteristics, following Dekle, Eaton and Kortum (2007). The first equation is income equal to expenditure in the counterfactual equilibrium: labor income in iii equals the sum over destinations of their expenditure on goods from iii, since goods expenditure in nnn equals wnLnw_nL_nwn​Ln​. The second is the trade share equation in changes, with productivities held fixed and L^i=λ^i\hat{L}_i=\hat{\lambda}_iL^i​=λ^i​ because total population is fixed. The third is the population share equation in changes, with productivities and land supplies held fixed. The three sets of equations are solved for {w^n,π^ni,λ^n}\{\hat{w}_n,\hat{\pi}_{ni},\hat{\lambda}_n\}{w^n​,π^ni​,λ^n​}. Given σ(1−α)>1\sigma(1-\alpha)>1σ(1−α)>1 and symmetric trade costs the equilibrium is unique, so the predictions are determinate.

Welfare

Consider a change in trade costs between an initial equilibrium (indexed by 0) and a subsequent equilibrium (indexed by 1). Because the expression for Vˉ\bar{V}Vˉ holds for every populated location in both equilibria, and fundamentals do not change, the change in the domestic trade share and in the population of any one location is a sufficient statistic for the welfare effect on all locations:

Vˉ1Vˉ0=(πnn0πnn1)ασ−1(λn0λn1)σ(1−α)−1σ−1(20)\frac{\bar{V}^1}{\bar{V}^0}=\left(\frac{\pi_{nn}^0}{\pi_{nn}^1}\right)^{\frac{\alpha}{\sigma-1}}\left(\frac{\lambda_n^0}{\lambda_n^1}\right)^{\frac{\sigma(1-\alpha)-1}{\sigma-1}} \tag{20}Vˉ0Vˉ1​=(πnn1​πnn0​​)σ−1α​(λn1​λn0​​)σ−1σ(1−α)−1​(20)

Given σ(1−α)>1\sigma(1-\alpha)>1σ(1−α)>1, a larger reduction in a location's domestic trade share must be offset by a larger increase in its population to preserve real wage equalization. If an infrastructure improvement reduces trade costs for one location by more than for others, the upward pressure on its real wage induces a population inflow until the price of immobile land is bid up enough to restore equality. The first factor is the analog of the result in the trade literature that the domestic trade share is a sufficient statistic for the gains from trade (Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare 2012). The second factor appears because, with an immobile factor used residentially, changes in the distribution of the mobile factor must also be taken into account.

Quantitative Illustration

The illustration uses a 30 by 30 grid of 900 locations divided into two countries, West and East, each occupying half of the grid. Labor is perfectly mobile within each country and immobile between them, so there is one common level of welfare per country. Following Donaldson (2016), trade costs are based on lowest-cost-route effective distance. Each point has a cost weight δn\delta_nδn​; an orthogonal link between neighbors has effective distance (δn+δi)/2(\delta_n+\delta_i)/2(δn​+δi​)/2 and a diagonal link has [2(δn+δi)2]0.5/2[2(\delta_n+\delta_i)^2]^{0.5}/2[2(δn​+δi​)2]0.5/2, and the weights are normalized to one. Productivities {An}\{A_n\}{An​} are independent draws from a standard lognormal distribution, and every location has the same quality-adjusted land area of 100 square kilometers. The land share 1−α1-\alpha1−α is 0.25, in line with the housing expenditure share in Davis and Ortalo-Magne (2011). The elasticity of substitution is σ=5\sigma=5σ=5, so the trade elasticity is σ−1=4\sigma-1=4σ−1=4, in line with Simonovska and Waugh (2014). Trade costs are a constant elasticity function of effective distance with elasticity ϕ\phiϕ, chosen so that the distance elasticity of trade flows is −(σ−1)ϕ=−1.5-(\sigma-1)\phi=-1.5−(σ−1)ϕ=−1.5, which gives ϕ=0.375\phi=0.375ϕ=0.375. Two economic frictions are added: a proportional internal tax of 100 percent, τin=2\tau^{in}=2τin=2, paid whenever a good flows from one location to another, and a proportional external tax of 100 percent, τout=2\tau^{out}=2τout=2, paid whenever a good crosses the border between the countries. Revenue from both taxes is wasted, so both are real resource costs.

  • Initial equilibrium: locations with high productivity have large populations, high wages and high land prices. The price index is a smooth surface with a gradient governed by trade costs; it is lowest at the two large cities close to the border and shows a discontinuity at the border.

  • External liberalization: removing the border tax reallocates activity toward the border. The largest gains in population, wages and land rents, and the largest reductions in the price index, occur close to the border on the side opposite the large cities. The largest agglomerations lose in relative terms. Welfare rises by about 0.2 percent in West and 0.3 percent in East.

  • Internal liberalization: removing the internal tax and keeping the border tax reduces the size of the two large cities in favor of rural areas, because lower trade costs weaken the home market effect that lowers price indices in large cities. Prices fall everywhere but less in populous areas, and wages and land rents fall in large agglomerations and rise elsewhere. Welfare rises by about 1.4 percent in West and 2.3 percent in East, more than five times the effect of external liberalization, because trade between regions is much larger than trade between countries.

Market Access and Evidence

The model links wages and prices to market access. A firm in location iii must sell xˉi\bar{x}_ixˉi​ to break even, and with CES demand this requires:

The sum on the right is firm market access FMAiFMA_iFMAi​ (Redding and Venables 2004), and substituting xˉi\bar{x}_ixˉi​ gives a wage equation; the price index is a function of consumer market access CMAnCMA_nCMAn​, in which pip_ipi​ is the free-on-board price in iii:

The paper collects the constant in the wage equation in a scalar that it again calls ξ\xiξ, although it is unrelated to the scalar of the same name above. Wages rise with productivity and with firm market access. Redding and Venables (2004) and Hanson (2005) find strong correlations between wages and market access across countries and across US counties. For causal evidence the review points to Redding and Sturm (2008), who use the division of Germany: West German cities close to the new border declined by about one third in relative size, and the model accounts for the average effect and for the larger effect on small cities at parameter values satisfying σ(1−α)>1\sigma(1-\alpha)>1σ(1−α)>1. The treatment effect depends on two parameter combinations, σ(1−α)\sigma(1-\alpha)σ(1−α) and (σ−1)ϕ(\sigma-1)\phi(σ−1)ϕ. Donaldson (2016) finds that the effect of Indian railroads on real income becomes insignificant after controlling for the own trade share, and Donaldson and Hornbeck (2016) find that without the railroads built up to 1890 the value of US agricultural land would have been about 60 percent lower. The elasticity of productivity with respect to density is typically estimated at 3 to 8 percent (Rosenthal and Strange 2004).

With LLL the measure of workers who choose the city, workplace and residence employment are the marginals of the commuting probabilities, LMi=∑nλniLL_{Mi}=\sum_n\lambda_{ni}LLMi​=∑n​λni​L and LRn=∑iλniLL_{Rn}=\sum_i\lambda_{ni}LLRn​=∑i​λni​L; the paper prints double sums over both indices in these two expressions, which is a misprint. Floor space is allocated between commercial and residential use by a no-arbitrage condition that allows for a tax equivalent of land use regulations. Because preferences are heterogeneous, each location faces an upward-sloping supply of residents and workers, with elasticity governed by ϵ\epsilonϵ. Without externalities (μ=η=0\mu=\eta=0μ=η=0) the congestion forces of commuting costs and inelastic land ensure a unique equilibrium (Ahlfeldt et al. 2015). With externalities there can be multiple equilibria, but given enough data on the endogenous variables the mapping to the unobserved fundamentals aia_iai​ and bnb_nbn​ can still be unique, so the model can be inverted; counterfactuals then require an equilibrium selection rule, for example the equilibrium closest to the observed one. Using the division and reunification of Berlin, Ahlfeldt et al. (2015) estimate μ=0.07\mu=0.07μ=0.07 and η=0.15\eta=0.15η=0.15, and the model without agglomeration forces cannot account for the observed reallocations. Monte et al. (2015) combine goods trade, migration and commuting in one framework, in which the local employment elasticity is heterogeneous across locations.

Extension: Dynamics

Most of the frameworks are static. Dynamics enter through sunk migration costs, which make location choices depend on expected continuation values (Artuc, Chaudhuri and McLaren 2010; Caliendo et al. 2015), and through innovation, where the spatial distribution of activity determines the market size of firms and so the return to local innovation (Desmet and Rossi-Hansberg 2014; Desmet, Nagy and Rossi-Hansberg 2016). The high dimensionality of the state space is the main difficulty. The innovation models stay tractable because a competitive land market together with local diffusion of technology implies that the future returns to an innovation are capitalized in land rents. The same argument is less attractive for capital, and a dynamic spatial model with local capital accumulation or with endogenous consumption-savings decisions and trade imbalances had not yet been developed. In these dynamic models the equilibrium is unique and the evolution of the economy is determined by initial conditions, so evidence of path dependence need not imply multiple equilibria. Running the dynamics of Desmet, Nagy and Rossi-Hansberg (2016) backwards from data for the year 2000 gives a correlation of 0.74 between actual and predicted country populations in 1950. The review lists services, dynamics, sorting of heterogeneous workers and firms, and the geography of firm and worker networks as areas for further research.

This block belongs to the urban model, in which α\alphaα and AiA_iAi​ have new meanings. The single final good is the numeraire and is produced under perfect competition and constant returns with labor share α\alphaα and commercial floor space share 1−α1-\alpha1−α. The first expression says that the unit cost in block iii equals the price of one: firms earn zero profits wherever production takes place. For a Cobb-Douglas technology the unit cost is wiαqi1−α/Aiw_i^{\alpha}q_i^{1-\alpha}/A_iwiα​qi1−α​/Ai​ times the constant α−α(1−α)−(1−α)\alpha^{-\alpha}(1-\alpha)^{-(1-\alpha)}α−α(1−α)−(1−α); the paper sets this constant to one, which amounts to a choice of units for AiA_iAi​. The second and third expressions split productivity into an exogenous fundamental aia_iai​ and an externality. Υi\Upsilon_iΥi​ is the sum of workplace employment densities LMs/KsL_{Ms}/K_sLMs​/Ks​ of all blocks, discounted by travel time τis\tau_{is}τis​ at rate δ>0\delta>0δ>0, and μ\muμ is the elasticity of productivity with respect to this density. With μ=0\mu=0μ=0 productivity is exogenous. This agglomeration force is technological, unlike the pecuniary one in equation (5), and it is the source of possible multiple equilibria. The parameters are identified by Ahlfeldt et al. (2015) from the changes in the surrounding density of each block caused by the division and reunification of Berlin, with μ=0.07\mu=0.07μ=0.07.

Residential amenities are modeled in the same way as productivity in equation (23). BnB_nBn​ is the amenity enjoyed by every resident of block nnn and enters utility in equation (25). bnb_nbn​ is the exogenous residential fundamental (for example scenic views), Ωn\Omega_nΩn​ is the travel-time-weighted sum of residence employment densities LRr/KrL_{Rr}/K_rLRr​/Kr​ of all blocks, and η\etaη is the elasticity of amenities with respect to this surrounding residential density. In this model ρ\rhoρ is the rate at which residential externalities decay with travel time τnr\tau_{nr}τnr​, not the CES parameter of equation (2).

Each weight e−ρτnre^{-\rho\tau_{nr}}e−ρτnr​ lies between zero and one and equals one for the block itself if own travel time is zero. A larger ρ\rhoρ means more localized spillovers; as ρ→∞\rho\to\inftyρ→∞ only own density matters and

Because BnB_nBn​ enters the commuting probability in equation (26) with exponent ϵ\epsilonϵ, residential externalities feed back into where people live. Ahlfeldt et al. (2015) estimate η=0.15\eta=0.15η=0.15. Given the parameters and observed data, the fundamental bnb_nbn​ is recovered as a residual, in the same way as HnH_nHn​ in the regional model.

The first expression is the indirect utility of worker ooo who lives in block nnn and works in block iii; the first subscript is always the residence and the second the workplace. It comes from Cobb-Douglas preferences over the final good, with share β\betaβ, and residential floor space, with share 1−β1-\beta1−β: income is the wage wiw_iwi​ earned at the workplace, the cost of living is Qn1−βQ_n^{1-\beta}Qn1−β​ because the final good is the numeraire, BnB_nBn​ is the residential amenity of equation (24), and κni=eκτni≥1\kappa_{ni}=e^{\kappa\tau_{ni}}\geq1κni​=eκτni​≥1 is an iceberg commuting cost that reduces utility proportionally and rises with travel time τni\tau_{ni}τni​.

The second expression is the distribution of the idiosyncratic shock znioz_{nio}znio​, drawn independently for every worker and every residence-workplace pair. The shape parameter ϵ\epsilonϵ governs dispersion; a larger ϵ\epsilonϵ means workers are more alike and respond more strongly to differences in wages, prices and commuting costs. The restriction ϵ>1\epsilon>1ϵ>1 makes the mean finite, which equation (27) needs.
